analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal minimum wage at what a full-time worker needs to support a family of four above poverty, adjusted every four years.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise the minimum wage to a living-wage level was referred to committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Labor Department to set the federal minimum wage at the hourly rate a person working 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year needs to earn 25.5% more than the federal poverty line for a family of four — far above the $7.25 minimum in effect. The rate would be recalculated every four years and could never be lowered. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action, no hearing, and no cosponsors before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would have seen the largest gains: the minimum wage would have been set well above the current $7.25 and adjusted upward automatically every four years, raising pay for millions of full-time workers whose earnings currently fall below the poverty line for a family of four. Their families and communities would also benefit, since the bill's own findings tie the change to housing affordability.

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Fair Labor Standards Act so the minimum wage equals what a person working full-time, year-round must earn to take home 25.5% more than the federal poverty threshold for a family of four — a level well above the then-current $7.25 minimum.
The Labor Department would recompute the wage every four years, and could never lower it, so the floor would rise with the cost of living instead of eroding between acts of Congress.

The bill's findings note that a full-time minimum-wage worker earns below the poverty line for a family of four, and that average rent for a one-bedroom apartment consumes more than 65% of a minimum-wage worker's monthly income.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that employ minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, care work, and other low-margin employers — would have borne higher payroll costs, and some economists argue a portion of that cost can come back as higher prices or fewer hours. Consumers could see some of those costs passed through.

drawbacks.text: The bill provides no phase-in or small-business accommodation: it ties the federal minimum wage directly to a poverty-threshold formula, which would mean a sharp, sudden increase in labor costs for employers, particularly small businesses and low-margin employers.

The formula fixes the wage to a family-of-four poverty benchmark nationwide, giving the Labor Department little flexibility to account for regional cost differences; a rate high enough for a family of four may be set differently than one calibrated to teenage or part-time workers.

Economists who accept a higher minimum wage generally favor gradual increases; this bill would have taken effect quickly (September 1, 2018 under the introduced text) and adjusted every four years by formula, removing Congress's step-by-step judgment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to low-wage workers would have been large — a minimum wage tied to what a family actually needs to afford food and housing, rather than a political number. The drawbacks are real: a large mandated wage increase falls heavily on small businesses and low-margin employers, could speed automation or reduced hours for the very workers it aims to help, and the formula (based on poverty thresholds for a family of four) may be a blunt instrument that fits some regions better than others. But none of these tradeoffs was ever tested through committee work, hearings, or a vote — the bill died on arrival, so its costs and benefits remain hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and stayed there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Al Green introduced the Original Living Wage Act in the House on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which has jurisdiction over the federal minimum wage.
No representative signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never took the bill up, and no further action was recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill would have raised the federal minimum wage to a living-wage level calculated from the poverty threshold for a family of four, recomputed by the Labor Department every four years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the federal minimum wage kept the status quo: no increase in labor costs, and no raise for their lowest-paid workers. No committee or leader had to defend killing the bill, since it never reached a vote.

for.name: Rep. Al Green
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 3, 2019 and took no further action on it for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Low-wage employers (retail, food service, hospitality, home care)
industries.note: The bill would have mandated substantially higher minimum pay for their lowest-wage employees, raising labor costs concentrated in these industries. Higher pay for workers would also mean somewhat more customer spending at these same businesses.

industries.industry: Businesses relying on the $7.25 federal wage floor
industries.note: Any employer paying the federal minimum would have had to raise wages to the new formula-based floor or lose workers, redistributing income from owners and higher-paid staff to the lowest-paid workers.
